Bologna has been operating as a university since 1088.

That is older than Magna Carta, older than most European countries, and older than the printing press by nearly 400 years.

The oldest university in each country — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ The darkest band is the medieval core: Bologna 1088, Oxford 1096, Salamanca 1134, Paris 1160, Coimbra 1290. These were rarely founded from nothing. Teaching guilds formed first; popes and kings chartered what already existed.

2/ Bologna began as a guild of students who hired their professors and could fire them. Paris was the mirror image — a guild of masters. Two rival answers to who actually runs a university, both about 900 years old, still unresolved.

3/ Central Europe arrives in one burst. Prague's Charles University 1348, Kraków's Jagiellonian 1364, Vienna 1365, Pécs 1367, Heidelberg 1386. In four decades the university crossed the Alps and stopped being a Mediterranean institution.

4/ A second wave follows the Reformation and the north's rise: Uppsala 1477, Copenhagen 1479, Leiden 1575, Vilnius 1579, Trinity College Dublin 1592, Tartu 1632. New states and new faiths needed their own men trained at home.

5/ The palest countries mostly tell you when the state arrived, not when learning did. Sofia 1888, Iceland 1911, Belarusian State University 1921. In the Balkans, independence and a national university tend to be the same project.

6/ The oddity is Luxembourg, where the map's oldest entry is a 1968 American outpost — Miami University's European centre. Luxembourg founded its own national university only in 2003, having sent its students abroad for centuries.

7/ Dates like these are always a little soft: charters, first lectures and refoundations all compete. But the pattern holds — the university is one of the few medieval institutions still doing its original job.
